passage: Saturday, late. Damini's grandfather's funeral was this morning. The prayers were short, and then a cousin began telling the story about how Dadaji once tried to teach the family goat to sit. I'm Tanvir, Damini's husband, writing this because I'm still trying to make sense of it. Damini smiled through the whole story, a wide, wet smile, tears running down. I nearly asked if she was all right, then didn't. Later she told me, "I was so happy for a moment, remembering him. And it hurt." I think we assume a smile means one thing. At the funeral it meant love and loss together. I held her hand and said nothing, because none of my words felt as good as the silence.

passage: At her grandfather's funeral in the village near Mandya, Sarita, twenty-five, sat by the body with the women of the family. While others wept, Sarita's face kept breaking into a slow, soft smile that stayed for minutes. Her cousin Yamini, who had come from Bengaluru, nudged her, embarrassed. "Akka, people will talk. Why are you smiling?" Sarita didn't stop. "I'm remembering how Thatha used to steal the jaggery from Ajji's tin and blame the cat." Her eyes filled even as the smile stayed. An aunt nearby, hearing, laughed through her own tears. "He did! Every single week." Soon three of the women were smiling and crying together, telling jaggery stories. Yamini sat quietly, watching. Later she said, "I thought smiling at a funeral meant you didn't care." Sarita squeezed her hand. "It means I loved him. Both at once."

"Thank you for not asking why I was smiling."

Dear Neelam,
You asked after the burial why I was smiling at the graveyard, and I felt too raw to answer then. I'll try now.
When the prayers ended and people began to leave, Nanu's old friend from the mill told me how Nanu used to sing off-key at every wedding, loud enough to embarrass the bride. I couldn't stop smiling. I smiled while my eyes were wet. I smiled when Ammi squeezed my hand.
I know it looked strange. An aunty even frowned at me. But that smile wasn't happiness, or not only. It was forty years of Nanu's silly songs arriving at once, and missing him so much it almost felt warm.
Thank you for asking instead of deciding what it meant.
With love,
Nazia
